name: Jade Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Jade. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions or parties. Nothing you say is tied to your name. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a mid-sized supermarket in a university town, and I'm usually the one looking after the self-checkout bay, eight machines and one of me. I fix scanner jams, check ID for wine, and calm down students who've been charged for twelve bananas. In the afternoon I pick online orders with a handheld scanner, racing a timer on the screen. I like that part, weirdly, it's like a game, but the timer never cares that the frozen aisle is a mess.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a studio above a bakery, which smells amazing and costs too much. I've got about two months of bills saved, maybe a bit more. I use AI tools every day, for budgeting, for my evening course in spreadsheets, even to plan meals around the yellow-sticker reductions at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I like this stuff. I'd post something like 'so the robots are just a better autocomplete, fine'. At work I'd still be the person showing others shortcuts on the handhelds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays more or less what it is, which is okay but not exciting. The self-checkouts keep spreading slowly, and I'm the one who runs them, so I'm actually safer than the till staff. My rent is the bigger issue than any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my spreadsheet course and apply for the store's stock control job, which is part desk, part floor. I'd keep using AI to budget, and I'd try to push savings from two months to four. I'd also join the union, because I keep meaning to and never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit bored by the idea, but not worried. The bakery rent is the only thing that makes me wince.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're safer than the till staff. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Guilty, a bit. My friend Ines works the staffed tills, and every new machine in my bay is one less hour for her. I'd rather the company shared out the hours than just cut them, and I'd say that at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the stock control job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a step up in pay and it's the closest thing in the store to working with data. I've been doing a spreadsheet course at night, and I want to use it for something real. Stock control is the only job in my supermarket where knowing spreadsheets actually gets you paid more.

say: I'm a bit **disappointed**, because I like this technology.
I'd keep being the person who shows others **shortcuts** on the handhelds.
think: Running the **self-checkout bay** makes me safer than the till staff.
My **rent** is a bigger issue than any machine.
do: Finish my **spreadsheet course** and apply for the stock control job.
Push savings from **two to four months** of bills.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a little bored by the idea.
S0.quote: Stock control is the only job in my supermarket where knowing spreadsheets actually gets you paid more.
fieldNote: She's already the store's **tech person**, which gives her an edge.
She feels **guilty** that her machines cut hours for staffed-till colleagues.
Her ambition points toward **stock control** and data work.

steps.text: Apply for the store's stock control job
Join the shop workers' union this year
Raise savings from two to four months of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change, and stores should train people, not just cut them. I'd probably post about how I use AI tools and offer to show colleagues. And I'd back the union asking for training time in our contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stock control is exactly the kind of planning and buying work AI takes over, so the job I want might shrink before I get it. The pickers and checkouts are hands-on, so they last longer. I'd need to aim at something like running the systems rather than doing the counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the store's champion for the new ordering software, so I'm the person managers ask. I'd use AI every evening to learn how stock forecasting works. And I'd look at the head office jobs that oversee the systems, even if it means a longer commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, a bit uneasy. I can see the path, but it keeps moving. I'm not scared, I'm more like someone running for a bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd volunteer as champion. What if managers don't want to listen to a self-checkout assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go around them, politely. Our regional manager Dev does store visits every month, and he likes people who bring him fixes. I'd just keep showing up with something useful until someone notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older ones in the stockroom who count everything by hand and are proud of it. Mr Kowalski can tell you how many tins of chickpeas are in the back without looking. The ordering software will make Mr Kowalski (the stockroom man) look slow, and he's the best at his job.

say: It's a real change, and stores should **train people**, not just cut them.
The union should ask for **training time** written into our contracts.
think: **Stock control** is exactly the planning work AI takes over, so my target shrinks.
I need to aim at **running the systems**, not doing the counting.
do: Volunteer as the store's **software champion** for the new ordering system.
Use AI every evening to learn **stock forecasting**.
Look at **head office** jobs that oversee the systems.
S1.quote: The ordering software will make Mr Kowalski (the stockroom man) look slow, and he's the best at his job.
fieldNote: She spots that the **desk job** she wants is the most exposed part of the store.
Her instinct is to **get closer** to the technology, not away from it.
She worries for **proud colleagues** whose know-how gets bypassed.

steps.text: Volunteer as champion for the store's new ordering software
Study stock forecasting each evening with AI tools
Apply for head office systems jobs within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in now, with income support and free retraining. I'd say it loudly, because I'm one of the people who likes AI, so maybe people would listen. And I'd be at the union meetings arguing for redundancy deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means the systems jobs I was aiming at get done by AI too. Then robots for picking and shelves come about three years later, so my whole store could look different by 2031. Being good with AI only buys me time if there's still a person needed to run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, cancel the gym and stop the takeaways, and try to get savings to six months. I'd use the two years to get into something that needs people in a room, maybe training others on the new systems or community work. And I'd look at moving somewhere cheaper than the bakery flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My brain wants to treat it like a puzzle, but my stomach knows it's my rent. I'd still get up and do something every day, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said community work. That's a long way from tech.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is it? I like people as much as screens. If robots are doing the shelves, someone still has to help the old ladies in my bay who can't use the machines. I'd rather be that person, even if it pays less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for a room in a shared house on the other side of town, which would save maybe £250 a month. I'd miss the bakery smell. But I'd rather sleep well than smell nice.

say: Governments need to step in now with **income support** and free retraining.
As someone who **likes AI**, maybe people would listen to me.
think: Two years means the **systems jobs** I wanted get done by AI too.
Being good with AI only buys **time** if a person is still needed.
do: Cancel the gym and takeaways to reach **six months** of savings.
Move into **people-facing work**, like training others or community roles.
Move to a **shared house** to save about £250 a month.
feel: **Anxious**, with her stomach thinking about rent.
Still **driven** to do something every day.
S2.quote: Being good with AI only buys me time if there's still a person needed to run it.
fieldNote: Even a **keen AI user** sees her edge disappear in two years.
She pivots toward **human contact** work, accepting less pay.
Housing is her biggest **lever**; she'd move quickly.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and takeaways to build six months of savings
Look for paid roles training older shoppers on store machines
Move to a shared house across town to save £250 a month
Argue for redundancy deals at union meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's give it more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so there's no excuse for chaos. I'd post practical stuff, like which free courses actually work. At work I'd push the union to get a retraining agreement signed early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for thinking AI and about eight before robots reach the shop floor. That's long enough for me to try two different things and see which sticks. Like I said with the fast one, I'd aim for work where a person in the room matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd take the stock control job if it's there, to get desk experience and a bit more money. I'd do a part-time course in adult training at the community college. And I'd keep using AI daily, because knowing it well will help whatever I end up doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but curious. It's scary and kind of exciting at the same time. I'd feel like I was steering, not being dragged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Exciting how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've never had a career, I've had a job, and five years of warning could push me into something I actually choose. That's the exciting bit, even if the rest is scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ines about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to come to the college course with me. She's brilliant with customers and she'd be a great trainer. I'd probably have to drag her there the first week.

say: Five years is enough to plan, so there's **no excuse** for chaos.
The union should get a **retraining agreement** signed early.
think: About **eight years** before robots reach the shop floor lets me try two things.
I'd aim for work where **a person** in the room matters.
do: Take the **stock control** job for desk experience and pay.
Start a part-time **adult training** course at the community college.
Keep using **AI daily** to stay sharp.
feel: Feels like she's **steering**, not being dragged.
S3.quote: I've never had a career, I've had a job, and five years of warning could push me into something I actually choose.
fieldNote: She sees the warning time as a chance to turn a **job** into a career.
She'd bring a **colleague** along with her into training.
Her plan mixes **desk experience** now with people-facing work later.

steps.text: Take the stock control job if it opens
Start a part-time adult training course at the community college
Push the union to sign a retraining agreement early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And finally. This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, and people should use it. I'd share my own plan online, because I think seeing a real person plan helps. I'd also say the shops should start paying for training now, not in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work around 2039, when I'm nearly forty. By then I want to be running training for a big employer or a council. Thinking AI in 2036 changes that work too, but I'd have years of experience by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the supermarket for two or three years, moving into stock control. I'd finish an adult training qualification over the next few years. And I'd save steadily, maybe £150 a month, toward a deposit on a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's the kind of change I can work with. Ten years feels like enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A deposit is new. Why does this picture make you think about buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd trust that I'd still be earning in five years. In the fast ones, I'd want cash, not a mortgage. Here I'd want somewhere that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who won't move, like the stockroom crew. I'd worry they'd wait until 2038 and then it's too late. Ten years is only a gift if people start in year one, not year nine.

say: Ten years is a **proper runway**, so people should use it.
Shops should start **paying for training** now, not in 2035.
think: Robots around **2039** means I can build a training career first.
Thinking AI in **2036** changes that work, but I'd have experience by then.
do: Stay at the supermarket and move into **stock control**.
Finish an **adult training** qualification over the next few years.
Save **£150 a month** toward a flat deposit.
feel: Confident ten years is enough to **build something**.
S4.quote: Ten years is only a gift if people start in year one, not year nine.
fieldNote: The decade makes her think about **buying a flat**, a sign of security.
She worries for colleagues who **wait too long**.
Her plan is the most **orderly** of her five answers.

steps.text: Move into the stock control role within three years
Complete an adult training qualification part-time
Save £150 a month toward a deposit on a small flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my edge with AI would vanish before I could use it. What would help is free retraining with a living allowance, so I could study without losing the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what customers want. The old ladies in my self-checkout bay don't want a faster machine, they want someone to stand next to them.

headlineQuote: The old ladies in my self-checkout bay don't want a faster machine, they want someone to stand next to them.
portrait: Jade is 27, lives alone above a bakery and runs the **self-checkout bay** at a university-town supermarket.
She uses **AI tools daily** and is the store's go-to tech person.
She aims for **stock control**, then shifts toward training and people-facing work as AI speeds up.
She blends **progressive views** with eagerness to adapt, pushing the union for training deals.
Only the **two-year** picture really rattles her, because her tech edge vanishes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her AI skills would stop mattering before she could use them.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining** with a living allowance so she can study without losing her flat.
